name: Maca (Lepidium meyenii)
short: Case report: blood lead rose on maca root powder and fell after stopping. 90-day trial: maca alone raised AST (a liver enzyme) and diastolic blood pressure. Report: restless legs with mianserin.
text: Lead exposure (case report): a woman whose raised blood lead had first been traced to a ceramic mug had a further rise a year later after she began taking a maca root powder supplement, and her levels fell again when she stopped it; the abstract does not give her blood lead during the maca period, describe symptoms or say whether the supplement was tested for lead. The authors say maca powder may contain lead and other minerals, and that consumers, particularly women of childbearing age, should be aware that imported products may contain significant amounts of lead. Liver enzyme and blood pressure: in a 90-day randomised placebo-controlled study in people with metabolic syndrome, volunteers taking maca alone had a moderate rise in AST (a liver enzyme) and in diastolic blood pressure, while no adverse effects were found in those taking silymarin alone or silymarin combined with yacon or with maca; the authors say the effect of maca on AST and blood pressure must be considered with high doses of maca powder. In contrast, in a 6-week-per-arm crossover trial in 29 postmenopausal Chinese women, diastolic blood pressure fell with maca. Interaction report: a retrospective review of 1,816 adverse-event reports found 30 in which an interaction between an antidepressant and a plant product containing adaptogens had a high probability of a causal relationship; one paired maca (Lepidium meyenii) with mianserin and restless legs syndrome. Trials: in a 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trial of red or black maca extracts in 175 adults living at low or high altitude, side effects were self-recorded, acceptability was good and no serious adverse effects were seen; black maca, and to a lesser extent red maca, lowered haemoglobin only in highlanders with abnormally high haemoglobin, and black maca lowered blood glucose. Two small trials of maca root in people with antidepressant-related sexual problems (45 women; 20 outpatients) describe it as well tolerated without giving adverse-event numbers, and a 2011 systematic review of 4 randomised trials in menopausal women states that the safety of maca has not been proved.
